# NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA): investment memo

**Avoid for now: $228.87 already pays for my base case.**

From the analyst to the portfolio manager (PM), the person who decides what the portfolio owns and in what size. Written 2026-09-23 from prices and filings as of the close on 2026-09-22.

**Action and size.** I recommend Avoid, which means owning none: 0% of the portfolio today. If the report due on 17 November passes two tests, I would buy 3.7%, half the full size of 7.4% that the portfolio's sizing rule gives NVIDIA.

**Return and risk.** I expect a return of 11.3% over 12 months, including $1.00 of dividends, against the 12.0% its risk requires. The bear case, the bad outcome I think plausible, loses 45.4%, and I give it one chance in four.

**Thesis.** NVIDIA's next year of earnings is well supported, but the price needs about as much growth as I forecast, so I would wait for two tests before buying.

**Why now.** The October-quarter report, due on 17 November, will show both tests: the company's own forecast for the quarter to January 2027, and whether customers are paying on time. The annual report in late February will show whether cash has caught up with profit.

## 1. THE DEBATE

NVIDIA's value turns on one question: whether spending on artificial intelligence data centers keeps growing through the fiscal year to January 2028 (FY2028). The filings support a high reading. Guidance, management's own published forecast, calls for October-quarter sales of $108.0 billion. NVIDIA has also signed $279 billion of supply commitments, contracts to buy parts and manufacturing capacity in the future. The same filings support a low reading. Three customers provided 44% of revenue in the first half, and cash from operations has lagged profit.

Over the next 12 months the price requires about the growth I forecast. To earn the 12% required return at today's multiple, it needs Data Center revenue to grow 30.2% in FY2028, and I forecast 32%.

Over ten years the price requires far more than any filing supports. Free cash flow (FCF) is the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment. A reverse DCF works backwards from the price to the growth it requires, and it needs FCF to grow 22.0% a year from FY2030 to FY2034. My base case slows that growth to 3% a year by FY2034.

## 2. MY VIEW

### NVIDIA's next year of earnings is well supported.

Management's own forecast and its purchase contracts point to another year of growth. Guidance for the October quarter is 12.2% above July. Supply commitments rose from $119 billion to $279 billion in a single quarter, which a company signs only for parts it expects to sell.

Profit is keeping pace with sales. Gross margin, revenue minus the cost of revenue as a share of revenue, was 75.0% in the July quarter against 72.4% a year earlier. Management credits a better mix of its newest systems.

I have no reason to think the price has missed any of this, because it all sits in the company's published forecast and quarterly report. Variant perception, where my forecast differs from what the price requires with a checkable reason the price has not yet moved, is therefore absent here.

### Cash is lagging profit, and a few customers account for the gap.

NVIDIA's profit is turning into cash more slowly than it did two years ago. Cash conversion, the share of profit that arrives as cash from operations, fell from 94% in FY2024 to 75% of adjusted profit in the first half of this year. Days sales outstanding (DSO), receivables divided by a quarter's revenue times 91 days, rose from 51 to 60.

The slower payments come from a small group of very large buyers. Three direct customers provided 44% of first-half revenue, and management attributes the longer collection times to extended payment terms on large agreements.

This is the risk I would most like to see settled before buying, and the October report will settle part of it. It is in the quarterly report, so I cannot claim the price has missed it. It sets my second test: DSO back at or below 55 days.

### The years after FY2029 cap what I would pay for the good case.

A discounted cash flow (DCF) model, which values a company as the sum of its future free cash flows each reduced to today's money, puts NVIDIA well below the price. At a 12% discount rate, the annual return required for the risk, and 3% growth after FY2034, mine gives $136 a share today.

I cannot test the long run within 12 months, so it does not set my recommendation. It does keep the bull case, the good outcome I think plausible, at one chance in four. It also sets a selling rule at the bull value, where the price would need even faster growth after FY2029.

| Required return | | | +12.0% | |

P/E, price divided by earnings per share (EPS), suits NVIDIA because its earnings are large, positive and forecast by management a quarter ahead. I apply it to EPS for the 12 months from September 2027. The base case holds today's multiple, the bull case uses about what Micron costs, and the bear case sits below every chip maker with positive earnings.

The probability-weighted value, each case's value multiplied by its probability with the results added, is $253.75. My price target, my estimate of what the shares will be worth in 12 months, is that value rounded to $255.

The required return, the annual return a stock must offer to pay for its risk, is set by how much NVIDIA's shares move with the market. The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) gives 12.0%, and the arithmetic is in SOURCES.

| Guidance for the January 2027 quarter | $108.0B for October | Below $108.0B, a fall from October | Stay out. If owned, Exit | 2026-11-17 |
| October-quarter revenue | $96.2B for July | Below $105.8B, the bottom of the guided range | Stay out. If owned, Exit | 2026-11-17 |
| DSO | 60 days | Above 70 days at the FY2027 year end | Stay out. If owned, Exit | Late February 2027 |
| Second-half cash conversion | 75% (first half) | 80% or more | If owned at half size, Add to 7.4% | Late February 2027 |
| Share price | $228.87 | $370, the bull value | If owned, Trim to half | Daily |

My view is wrong if NVIDIA grows faster than I assume while its customers pay on time. A falsifier is a specific, dated observation that would show a view is wrong. Mine is guidance of $125 billion or more for the January quarter, with DSO at or below 55 days. Both are due on 17 November, and if both happen I recommend Initiate.

A fall in the price alone is never an exit rule. It starts a review of the case values.

The strongest case against Avoid is that NVIDIA grows faster than any chip maker except Micron at a lower P/E than most. On that reading the cash gap is only the timing of large contracts. I accept most of it, which is why the expected return is positive and the tests can be met within eight weeks. The view survives because the return still falls short of what the risk requires until the tests are met.

## 5. RISKS

1. **Customer financing.** Several buyers must raise money to pay NVIDIA, and NVIDIA backs some of them, including a guarantee of up to $105 billion on a campus leased to OpenAI. The first sign of strain would be DSO rising further in the October report.
2. **Parts bought ahead of demand.** If orders slow, part of the supply commitments would become an inventory write-down, a charge for goods that can no longer be sold at cost, as happened in FY2023. The first sign would be guidance that falls from one quarter to the next while commitments keep rising.
3. **Export rules.** Rules on sales to China have already cost NVIDIA a charge this year, and guidance assumes no data center compute sales there. The first sign of wider harm would be a further charge, or a cut to guidance that names export rules.

## 6. WHAT I DO NOT KNOW

The gaps that could change my recommendation concern customers and the long run.

- No analyst forecasts are available, so I cannot say whether my figures sit above or below what other analysts expect.
- I cannot see which customers owe the $63.1 billion of receivables, or how much of NVIDIA's equity investments sit in its customers.
- No filing covers the years after FY2029, and the DCF depends on them more than on anything else.
- The probabilities are my judgment, and the recommendation turns on them as much as on the model.
- The required return rests on a 13-week Treasury bill in place of a 10-year yield. A beta of 1.46 in place of my 1.61 would close the gap between my expected and required returns.

## GLOSSARY

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Base case | The middle outcome the analyst thinks plausible, built from stated assumptions. |
| Bear case | The bad outcome the analyst thinks plausible, built from stated assumptions. |
| Beta | How much a stock tends to move for each 1% move in the market. |
| Bull case | The good outcome the analyst thinks plausible, built from stated assumptions. |
| Capital asset pricing model (CAPM) | A formula that sets the required return at the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium. |
| Cash conversion | The share of profit that arrives as cash from operations. |
| Days sales outstanding (DSO) | Receivables divided by a quarter's revenue, times 91 days. |
| Discount rate | The annual return an investor requires for the risk, used to reduce future cash to today's money. |
| Discounted cash flow (DCF) | A model that values a company as the sum of its future free cash flows, each reduced to today's money. |
| Earnings per share (EPS) | The profit attributable to each share. |
| Exit rule | A condition, stated before buying, under which the analyst would sell or cut a holding. |
| Expected return | The percentage gain from the last close to the probability-weighted value, plus any dividends expected over the same 12 months. |
| Falsifier | A specific, dated observation that would show a view is wrong. |
| Fiscal year (FY) | The twelve months a company's accounts cover. |
| Free cash flow (FCF) | The cash left after running the business and paying for equipment. |
| Gross margin | Revenue minus the cost of revenue, as a share of revenue. |
| Guidance | Management's own published forecast. |
| Inventory write-down | A charge for goods that can no longer be sold at cost. |
| P/E | Price divided by earnings per share. |
| Portfolio manager (PM) | The person who decides what the portfolio owns and in what size. |
| Price target | The analyst's estimate of what the shares will be worth in 12 months. |
| Probability-weighted value | Each case's value multiplied by its probability, with the results added. |
| Required return | The annual return a stock must offer to pay for its risk. |
| Reverse DCF | Working backwards from the price to the growth it requires. |
| Supply commitments | Contracts to buy parts and manufacturing capacity in the future. |
| Variant perception | Where the analyst's forecast differs from what the price requires, with a checkable reason the price has not yet moved. |
